title: The Incidence of Mandated Maternity Benefits
research_question: To what extent are the costs of mandates that raise the expense of employing a demographically identifiable group passed through to that group's wages, as opposed to producing changes in their employment and hours? Specifically, when laws require comprehensive insurance coverage for childbirth—raising the relative cost of insuring women of childbearing age and their husbands—how are wages, hours, and employment of the affected workers altered?
data_description: The study uses the May Current Population Survey for 1974, 1975, 1977, and 1978 to analyze state-level law changes, and the March CPS for 1978, 1979, 1981, and 1982 (covering labor-market data for 1977, 1978, 1980, and 1981) to analyze the federal law change. The unit of observation is the individual wage-earner aged 20–65 (excluding the self-employed and those with wages below $1 or above $100/hour in 1978 dollars). Key variables include log hourly wages, weekly hours, employment status, demographics (age, sex, marital status, race, education), union status, and industry. Auxiliary data come from the 1977 National Medical Care Expenditure Survey (about 2,900 women aged 20–40 with employer-based insurance), the 1979 May CPS Pension Supplement on insurance coverage, and a national insurer's small-group premium-pricing program providing age- and coverage-type-specific costs of adding maternity benefits.
institutional_context: Before the mid-1970s, U.S. employer-provided health insurance commonly treated childbirth less generously than other medical conditions—either excluding maternity coverage or paying only flat lump-sum amounts—while covering comparable illnesses comprehensively. Between 1975 and 1979, 23 states enacted laws prohibiting differential treatment of pregnancy in health insurance benefits. The analysis focuses on three early-adopting states (Illinois, New Jersey, and New York), whose laws took effect between July 1976 and January 1977, comparing them with neighboring states that did not enact such laws (Ohio, Indiana, Connecticut, Massachusetts, and North Carolina). In October 1978, the federal Pregnancy Discrimination Act extended similar requirements nationwide, prohibiting any differential treatment of pregnancy in employment. Estimated annual costs of adding maternity coverage ranged from under 1% to nearly 5% of weekly earnings depending on demographic group and coverage type, making these mandates economically significant for insured workers of childbearing age.
